en: *The Sutra on the Original Arising of the Bodhisattva*, one fascicle;
translated by the Western Jin layman Nie Daozhen.
When Śākyamuni Buddha was in a previous life as a human being, he was in the kingdom of Pukkuṣadharma.
Practicing goodness life after life, it is only after countless eons that one attains Buddhahood.
When the Buddha was a bodhisattva, he was known as a māṇava; he dwelt in the mountains, wearing garments of deerskin.
At that time, he entered a city named Pāṭaligrāma, where the king was named Jayasena.
Seeing the bustle within the city, the Bodhisattva asked a traveler on the road,
"Why is there such a rush in the city today?"
The practitioner replied,
"The Buddha shall come today!
Upon hearing that the Buddha was coming, the Bodhisattva felt joy within his heart alone and spoke these words:
"Those who see the Buddha coming today wish to seek from the Buddha the fulfillment of the desires in their hearts.
After a short while, there was a woman named Gopī who carried a ritual water flask and seven flowers; the flowers were called *utpala*.
The Bodhisattva followed her and called out,
"Sister, please stop! Jivī immediately stopped and waited for him.
The Bodhisattva said,
"Please give me the utpala flower from your hand,
lady. Gopī replied:
"The Buddha shall arrive today; the Great King is in the bathhouse, and I intended to offer him flowers.
But the flowers cannot be obtained.
The Bodhisattva said:
"I will pay one hundred coins for the flowers. Jivaka replied,
"The flowers cannot be obtained."
The Bodhisattva said,
"You may take it yourself. Jīvī replied:
"It cannot be obtained.
The Bodhisattva spoke again:
"I will pay five hundred coins for the flowers."
Kūṭadantī thought to herself:
"These flowers were originally worth only two or three coins, yet now they are being hired for five hundred.
She then gave him five *utpala* flowers, keeping two for herself.
The Bodhisattva reached into his breast and took out five hundred coins, giving them all to him; they then parted ways.
Jivaka thought to himself:
"This practitioner wears only deerskin robes, yet he just now had five hundred silver coins which he spent entirely to purchase these flowers; I suspect he is no ordinary man."
He immediately called out after him, saying:
"Young man, young man! Stop for a moment!"
The Bodhisattva then stopped and waited for her.
Ghṛtācī said, "If you tell me the truth, I shall give these flowers to you."
"If you do not, I shall take your flowers from you.
The Bodhisattva said, "I have purchased these flowers for a price ranging from one hundred up to five hundred coins; why do you take my flowers from me?"
Kubjā said, "These are the flowers of the royal household; by my power and influence, I can seize them from you.
The Bodhisattva then informed her of the truth.
"I have heard that the Buddha will arrive today; I wish to offer him flowers and seek from the Buddha whatever heart's desire I may have.
Jīvī said, "Excellent!"
"I vow that in a future life I shall become your wife; and in whatever future life you may be born, whether in good or evil circumstances, I shall become your wife.
I must fix my heart so that the Buddha may know it."
The Bodhisattva said, "Very well!
He then took two flowers from his hand and gave them to the Bodhisattva, instructing him to offer them to the Buddha.
Kubjā said, "As a woman, I am unable to go forward; I wish to entrust these flowers to you.
The Bodhisattva then accepted them, and they each departed on their separate ways.
In a brief moment, the Buddha arrived; from the king down to the common people, all scattered a hundred kinds of various flowers over the Buddha’s head, and the flowers all fell to the ground.
The Bodhisattva took five flowers and scattered them over the Buddha’s head; the flowers all remained suspended, arranged upward in rows like sprouting roots, without falling to the ground.

The Bodhisattva then took *kubjaka* flowers and scattered them over the Buddha’s head; these flowers likewise remained suspended, arranged upward in rows, resting upon his two shoulders without falling to the ground. The Buddha knew that the Bodhisattva’s resolve was sincere.
The Buddha said:
"As for the wish in your heart that you desire to fulfill, ninety kalpas hence, in a kalpa named Bhadra, you shall become Śākyamuni Buddha."

Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the Bodhisattva was filled with great joy in his heart; he immediately spread out his hair for the Buddha to tread upon, and thus stood before the Buddha, leaping for joy.
The Buddha received him with his supernatural power, causing him to rise four *zhang* and nine *chi* above the ground; without anything to support him, he descended from above.
The Buddha spoke again:
"In future lives, may you attain the Way and transcend the world, and likewise become a Buddha just as I am."
At that time, the Buddha was a Buddha of a previous age named Tishya Krakucchanda Buddha.

After that Buddha had entered parinirvāṇa, the Bodhisattva returned to the mountains; when his life there ended, he was reborn above in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where all the devas together protected and watched over him.
When his lifespan in the heavens came to an end, he descended again to be born in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī as a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin), ruling over the four continents.
At the end of his life, he was reborn above in the second heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa, where he became Śakra.
In this manner, dying and being reborn again and again, he served as Śakra, Lord of Devas, thirty-six times and as a Cakravartin Emperor eighty-four thousand times.

After his life has thus come to an end, he will immediately ascend to be born in the fourth heaven, Tuṣita; he will then descend again to be born in the kingdom of Kapilavastu—Kapilavastu being the very center of heaven and earth!
When the Buddha was born, it could not have been in a remote land or another country, for the earth would have tilted and slanted.
King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu was a man of benevolence and virtue; thus, [the Bodhisattva] descended into the womb of the Queen. However, because of impurities, there was no place for him to settle.

The ministers on both sides and the neighboring states, those who had requested that [the child] be assigned to the kingdom of Kapilavastu, hearing that the Queen was pregnant, all came to congratulate the Great King and prostrated themselves before her.
The Prince saw those outside from within his womb, as if looking through a fine gauze curtain.
When those outside paid their respects, the Prince reached out with his hand from within the womb and brushed them away.
Why did they ward it off? It was because they did not wish to trouble or disturb the people of the world.
When the Lady was carrying the Prince in her womb, the various deities of the heavens daily brought celestial food and placed it before the Lady.
The lady did not know where her food came from;
she could no longer eat the meals of the royal household, for the royal meals were bitter and pungent.

On the eighth day of the fourth month, at the hour of midnight, the Prince was born, emerging from his mother’s right side. As he fell to the ground, he took seven steps; his feet were raised four inches high and did not touch the earth. He then raised his right hand and spoke:
"In heaven above and on earth below, there is none more venerable than I!

As he spoke, the Four Heavenly Kings descended immediately to pay homage; they took up the Prince, placed him upon a golden table, and bathed his body with warm water, causing the King, the Queen, and their attendants to be struck with amazement.

When the Prince was born, from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above down to the sixteen hells below, and across the eight extremities of the world throughout twelve thousand worlds of heaven and earth, all were filled with great radiance; heaven and earth shook for this reason as he descended to become a child.
His wet nurse presented a cotton cloth bag to his mother, and she herself then nursed him.
He was named Siddhārtha; at birth, his body possessed the thirty-two marks of a great man.
The next day, the King consulted with his consort:
"My son’s birth was unlike that of others. In our kingdom there is a great man of the Way, over a hundred years of age, a master physiognomist whose name is Ayi."
"It would be better for us both to go together to see the Crown Prince. The lady said, "Very well!"
The king and his consort went together to the place where the practitioner was.
The king offered a bag of gold and a bag of silver to the practitioner; however, the practitioner would not accept the gold and silver, and instead opened the cotton cloth and looked at it.
The Crown Prince possessed the thirty-two marks and manifested divine radiance, whereupon the practitioner immediately wept and grieved.
The King’s consort asked:
"O practitioner! Why do you weep?"
"What unwholesome thing could you possibly have done?
Today the King has specifically selected you as his crown prince, wishing to know whether you are good or evil; for what reason do you weep?
The practitioner said:
"Yesterday, when heaven and earth shook, it was precisely for the sake of the Prince!

I lament my old age; now I am about to depart from this world. I regret not having waited for this man, and I regret not having heard this person's discourses on the sutras and precepts; for these reasons, I weep."

Upon hearing the words of the ascetic, the king immediately selected four thousand renowned courtesans from within the kingdom for the crown prince; he ordered that one thousand of them perform songs and music at a time, day and night without ceasing.

Furthermore, wishing to provide guard-duty for the Prince, the King, knowing well that artisans were skilled in physiognomy, immediately had the Prince’s palace, gates, and walls renovated; he ensured they were all complete and sturdy, such that when they were opened, the sound of the gatekeepers would be heard for forty *li*.
When the Prince was born, a servant also appeared in the palace, and a white horse also appeared; the servant’s name was Chandaka, and the horse’s name was Kaṇṭhaka.
The king ordered a servant to attend the Prince’s horse, to care for and protect it, and to ride it when needed.
Seven days after the Prince was born, his mother passed away.
When the Crown Prince was ten years old, he approached the Great King and said,
"As the King's crown prince, I have never yet gone out on an excursion. The King said:
"Excellent! he said, and immediately ordered his attendants and the hundred officials to follow the Prince on his excursion.

As the Prince rode out through the eastern city gate in his carriage, Śakra, the King of the second heaven, Trāyastriṃśa, immediately manifested himself as a sick man walking before him, with a distended belly and swollen body, his flesh and muscles completely wasted away, leaning against a wall to catch his breath.
The Prince asked his charioteer,
"What kind of person is this?
The charioteer replied:
"This is a person who is ill.
The Prince asked,
"In what way is one a person who is ill?"

The charioteer replied, "This man committed evil in his past lives; though he has now been born as a human, he was immoderate in eating and drinking, irregular in his sleep and rising, and thus fell ill."
The Prince said, "I am the son of the king;
if my diet is irregular and my sleep and rising are inconsistent, would I not likewise contract this illness?
The charioteer replied:
"Everyone must inevitably undergo this.
The Prince immediately turned his chariot around and returned; filled with sorrow and finding no joy, he thought:
"All people in the world shall surely fall ill; now I too shall become ill and shall no longer take food or drink."

The Great King regretted having allowed the Prince to go out on an excursion; he closed the palace gates again and would not let him out, instead providing him with performances of singing, dancing, and music.
The Prince’s grief and anxiety grew even more intense, such that he could neither eat nor drink; however, later on, he gradually recovered.
After several more years, the Prince again informed the Great King:
"Having been confined within the palace for a long time now, I long to go out on a tour once more.
The Great King, unable to bear the thought of contradicting the Prince's wishes, consented once again and issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom in advance:
"The Prince is about to go out; do not allow sick people or those who are unclean to be by the roadside.
Having thus instructed them all, he ordered the Prince to mount his carriage again and depart through the southern city gate.

Śakra, King of Devas, again transformed himself into a patient suffering from a fever; his hair and face were disheveled, he was smeared with excrement and urine, and lay prostrate upon them, his life hanging by a thread.
The Crown Prince asked the charioteer,
"What kind of person is this?
The charioteer replied:

"This person committed evil in his past lives and was unwilling to discipline himself; he was immoderate in eating and drinking, and irregular in his sleep and rising. Consequently, he has contracted this illness, and his life hangs by a thread."
The Prince said, "I too have been irregular in my diet and inconsistent in my sleep and rising; should I not contract this illness?
The charioteer replied:
"All people are subject to illness.
Thereupon, the Prince turned his chariot back again; once more he was filled with sorrow and anxiety, refusing to eat or drink.
The Great King said:

"Since you were my attendants at my side, I previously issued a decree throughout the kingdom that those who are ill or otherwise impure should not come before the Crown Prince; for what reason have you allowed the sick to see the Prince?"

"Later, they provided him with performers and music for the Crown Prince, but the Crown Prince remained sorrowful and could not find relief; he did not take pleasure in the music, and only after some time did he gradually recover.
After he had recovered for several years, the Crown Prince again informed the Great King:
'I am unhappy being confined within the palace and wish to go out on an excursion once more.'"
The king said, "Ever since you first came out, you have constantly been sorrowful and unhappy, having no desire for food or drink; why then do you go out on excursions again?"
The Prince said, "I shall not do so again.
The King then issued another decree throughout the kingdom:
"The Prince wishes to go out on an excursion; do not let any sick people or those who are unclean be seen by him on the road.
The Prince mounted his carriage and departed through the western city gate.
Śakra, King of Devas, again manifested himself as an old man, emaciated and hunchbacked, walking along while leaning upon a staff.
The Prince asked the charioteer,
"What kind of person is this?
The charioteer replied:
"This is an old man. The Prince asked,
"In what way is he an old man?"
The charioteer said:

"When a person is born upon this earth and reaches the end of their years, their lifespan comes to its close, their physical strength and vigor decline, and they are unable to eat or drink; therefore, one is called an 'old man.'"
The Prince asked,
"Am I also destined to grow old?
The charioteer replied:
"All living beings must grow old.
The Prince said, "Turn back the chariot and return; I, too, shall not remain long in this world."
He then became deeply distressed, thinking:
"All people must likewise grow old and decline; their food and drink will be exhausted, and they shall meet their end. Why should I remain long in this world?"
He refused to eat or drink, sitting dejected with his head bowed in sorrow.
The Great King again consoled and exhorted him:
"I have only you, my one son; I shall entrust the kingdom to you. Why, having gone out but once, do you return in such distress, refusing food and drink?"
The king provided him with great music to entertain him, and after some time, the [yakṣa] gradually grew weary of it.
After a long period had passed in this way, he again informed the king:
"I wish to go out for a stroll."
The king replied:

"Ever since you first came out, you have been constantly sorrowful and unhappy, refusing food and drink, and falling into a state of emaciation from which you nearly died. Why do you wish to go out on excursion again?"
The Prince said, "When I grow older, I shall also grow old.

The King again sent him out through the northern city gate. Śakra, the Heavenly King, again transformed himself into a funeral carriage, with men and women from both inside and outside the city holding banners and wailing as they followed the carriage to escort it away.
The Crown Prince asked his charioteer,
"What kind of human voice is this?
The charioteer replied:
"This is the sound of weeping.
The Prince asked,
"What kind of sound is this weeping?"
The charioteer said,
"There is someone who has died. The Prince said:
"What is death? the driver replied, "When a person lives upon this earth, their life is entrusted to Heaven; as there is length and brevity to one's lifespan, it is called death."
"The dead have no further consciousness; their bodies completely dissolve and vanish, never to return. Their families mourn in grief and follow them in funeral procession.
The Prince asked, "Am I also destined to die?"
The charioteer said,
"All people must return to death.
The Prince said:
"I cannot dwell long between heaven and earth; I shall return to this death.
He then turned his chariot and returned.
The King asked the driver:
"Why has the Prince returned so quickly?
His attendants replied, "While the Prince was out on an excursion, he saw a funeral procession on the road; his heart became distressed, and therefore he returned in haste."
The king said, "I,
too, do not wish for the prince to go out on excursions.
When the prince was twenty years old, the king wished to take a wife for him.
The Crown Prince said,
"I will not take a wife. The King,
for the sake of the Crown Prince, searched through all the women in the kingdom and found several hundred thousand, ordering the Prince to examine them with his own eyes.
Having finished looking at them, there was none who could satisfy the Crown Prince’s wishes.
Finally, there was a girl named Gopī, and the Crown Prince said:
"I wish to marry this girl."
The king then took her as a wife for the crown prince.
Regarding this woman whom he wedded for the prince—she who had previously sold flowers to the Bodhisattva in her past life, named Kūyi then, she continued to be named Kūyi in this present life.
The Prince said to his wife, "We two lie upon the same bed with our heads together; would it not be well to obtain some fine flowers and place them between us so that we may look at them together?"
His wife said, "The flowers can be obtained.
She immediately took the flowers and placed them in the center, and the husband and wife lay down on either side of them.
The woman’s intention was to become the consort of the Crown Prince, but the Crown Prince firmly told her:
"If you come to be with me, you must press these flowers; these flowers have sap that will flow and soil my bed and mats."
His wife then withdrew. After a long time, he spoke to his wife again:
"The two of us lie on the same bed with our heads together; I wish to obtain a fine cotton cloth and place it between us so that we may gaze upon it—would that not be pleasant?"
The wife said,
"Cotton cloth can be obtained.
She immediately took some cotton cloth and spread it out in the center.
The woman’s intention was to draw herself close to the Prince;
the Prince said, "If you come to cling to me, your sweat and grime will surely soil my fine cotton cloth."
The wife immediately withdrew and did not dare draw near to the Prince; suspecting him, she remained by his side, following him wherever he sat or rose.
At midnight, the Four Heavenly Kings came through the skylight and called out to the Prince, saying, "The time has come; you may depart."
The Prince said, "I wish to depart, yet I am unable to do so. Thereupon,
the Four Heavenly Kings caused the dancers and singers to fall into a deep slumber, such that they were no longer conscious of anything.
His wife lay down and fell asleep; the Prince slowly leaned against the bed, rose to look at her, and fearing she might wake up, he then descended from the bed and departed.
He called out to the attendant Chandaka, who was born on the same day as himself, ordering him to saddle the white horse Kanthaka in the middle courtyard.
Chandaka immediately saddled the horse; the Prince mounted it and intended to depart, but fearing that the gate might make a sound, he paced back and forth in the courtyard.
The sound of the Prince’s horse’s hooves was always heard for twenty *li*, and the sound of the gate opening was heard for forty *li*; therefore, the Prince did not dare open the gate.

The Four Heavenly Kings then commanded various spirits and deities to take hold of the horse’s hooves, leap over the walls, and exit the city, proceeding on their own to the royal family’s estate where they halted beneath a tree.
The next day, the king did not know where the crown prince was; there was commotion within the palace, and the king said:
"My son has never gone out on excursions before; he must currently be at the hunting lodge."
The king then went in person to the farmstead and saw from afar the prince sitting beneath a tree.
As the sun’s rays were about to shine upon the prince, the tree bent its branches and leaves to fan him, preventing the sunlight from falling on him.
The king, his heart filled with fear and alarm, dismounted and prostrated before the prince; the prince likewise prostrated before the king.
The prince said, "As your son, I have never gone out on excursions before; yet now that I have gone out for one, you, O King, pursue me again."
"My horse and servant remain by your side; I pray that Your Majesty return to the palace, and I shall return on my own in a few days.
The King immediately mounted his horse and returned home, saying to his wife, Kūyi:
"The Prince is currently at the hunting grounds; he will return in a few days."

The Prince sat beneath the tree, single-mindedly and deeply contemplating the events of successive kalpas; from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above down to the sixteen hells below, he found not a single thing that was acceptable.
He saw plowmen in the fields turning up earthworms from the soil—some were wounded, some were dead—and crows followed them to devour them.
The Prince sighed and said,
"When humans are born upon this earth, they must enter the hells upon death— is this not suffering!
I cannot dwell long in this world."
He immediately mounted his horse and departed.

After traveling ten or so li, he saw a man named Bishi—Bishi was a great deity among the ghosts and spirits, known for being fierce and irascible—who stood blocking the road. He held a bow in his left hand and an arrow in his right, with a sharp sword girded at his waist.
There are three paths established within the realm of consciousness:
first, the path of the devas; second, the path of human beings; and third, the path of the hell-beings and evil persons.
The Crown Prince saw him from afar and felt a sense of unease; he urged his horse straight toward him.
Bhīṣmaka was immediately seized with terror and trembling; he unsheathed his sword and took up his bow and arrows, then stepped back from the path and stood there.
The Crown Prince asked,
"Which path may I follow?
Pṛṣṭhapāla immediately showed him the way to the heavenly realm.
"This path may be taken.
After the Prince had traveled several li, he encountered a hunter on the road.
The Prince said, "I wish to borrow something from you; would it be possible?"
The hunter said, "What you seek can be obtained. The Prince said:
"I wish to obtain your deer skin.
The hunter immediately gave the skin to the Prince, and the Prince likewise gave him precious objects.
After the Prince had traveled several *li*, he halted his horse and dismounted, saying to Chandaka:
"If you return from here," Chanda said,
"I shall follow the Great Lord; I cannot return."
The Prince said, "Return and offer my thanks to the Great King and my wife, saying that I wish to enter the mountains to practice the Way and shall never return for the rest of my life.
The Prince took the jeweled crown from his head and the precious robes he wore upon his body, handing them to Chandaka; Chandaka wept as he accepted them.
The white horse knelt with its forelegs bent and shed tears as it licked the Prince’s feet.
Chandaka led the horse back on foot, weeping; the white horse also wept. Looking back from behind at the Prince, who had taken a deer skin to change his attire, they both grieved.

The wife, looking every day for the Prince’s return, instead saw only the empty horse; she wept and threw herself down at the foot of the palace steps, then embraced the horse's neck and said to Chandaka, "Where is the Prince?"
Chanda said, "The Prince sends his greetings to the Great King and my wife, saying: 'I have entered the mountains to practice the Way; I shall never return again for the rest of my life.'"
Kūṭadantī said: "How unfortunate I am!
Now that my husband is as if lost, where shall I seek him?"
"My husband! My husband!
Is he in heaven, beneath the earth, or among men?
I shall go forth to seek him!"
He spoke to the white horse, saying, "The Prince has departed with you; how could you return empty-handed?
Those around him were all moved to emotion.
When the King heard that the Crown Prince had departed, his tears fell in profusion, and he said to Jīvaka:
"In this world of men, all must eventually return to death; that my son has studied the Way to transcend the world—is this not excellent!"
He wished thereby to resolve Gopī’s mind. The King also thought incessantly of the Prince;

he then invited the wise and learned men of the kingdom, obtaining several thousand. From among those several thousand, he selected several hundred; from among those several hundred, he obtained several dozen; and from among those several dozen, he chose five men.
The King summoned the five men and asked them, "When you are at home day and night, embracing your children and holding your grandchildren, do you find joy in that alone?

Now I have an only son who has never gone abroad; he knows nothing of the world’s right and wrong. If one day he were to abandon me and travel far away into famous mountains, wandering through deep forests and crossing over streams and valleys, who would know of his hardships from cold, heat, hunger, and thirst?"
"Furthermore, there may be matters of good or ill fortune involving tigers, wolves, or fierce beasts; who among you would witness such things?
Now, each of you five shall send one son to search for my child; whoever finds him shall attend upon him."
"My son will never return for the rest of his life; you five men have abandoned my son midway and departed. I shall exterminate your families!
The five men immediately dispatched their five sons to search for the Prince. They found him on a famous mountain and followed him there to serve him.
Thus many years passed, yet the Prince did not ask the five men where they had come from.
The places where the Prince traveled were all deep, secluded forests; the five men grew weary and distressed by this, and said to one another:

"This Prince does not practice the Way of Study; he is merely suffering from madness. He wanders without choosing his path, and we five cannot follow him. If we return, the King will destroy our families; it would be better to stop here."
The five men all said, "We may!

The place where the five men stayed was by a large body of water; upon that water grew various kinds of fruits and gourds, which they could always eat throughout both winter and summer, and thus they did not suffer from hunger.
The five men remained behind, and the Prince did not inquire after them.
The Prince then entered a deep mountain, a place devoid of people; he gathered high grass from the ground and sat upright beneath a tree, single-mindedly resolving within himself:
"Today, though my flesh, bones, sinews, and marrow all wither and decay, I shall not rise from this spot until I have attained Buddhahood."
The Prince then attained the first dhyāna, then the second dhyāna, then the third dhyāna, and then the fourth dhyāna.
Within a single night, he attained *abhijñā* (supernormal knowledge) and came to know his own past lives through countless eons, from which he had previously arisen.

During the second watch of the night, he attained the second supernormal power, the divine eye; his vision was penetrating and all-pervading without limit, and he knew the births and deaths of beings and the paths they followed toward good or evil.
As dawn approached, he immediately attained Buddhahood.
The Buddha thought to himself: "I have become a Buddha!"
"It is difficult to encounter, difficult to know, and difficult to comprehend.
Having attained the Way of the Buddha, he went to the place where the dragon lived; the dragon’s name was Muḷāla.
Beside the water where Muḷāla resided there was a tree, and the Buddha sat upright beneath it and thought to himself:
"In the past, incalculable kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Dīpaṃkara who said, 'I shall become Śākyamuni Buddha,' and today I have already attained Buddhahood!"
"Since countless kalpas past, I have sought Buddhahood; it is only now that I have finally attained it!
Since countless kalpas past, all that I have practiced in giving was for the sake of entering the six pāramitās; do not forget my merit, for I have now fully realized it all."
As soon as the Buddha had this thought, he entered the *dhyānapāramitā*.
Sitting in meditation by the water beneath a tree, his radiance entered the water and illuminated the dwelling place of the nāga.
When the dragon saw the Buddha’s radiance, he was greatly startled, and the hair on his body and his scales stood erect.
In the past, this Dragon-Monk had already seen three Buddhas:
the first was named Krakucchanda Buddha; the second was named Kanakamuni Buddha; and the third was named Kāśyapa Buddha.
All were seated beneath the trees, and their reflections entered the water, illuminating the dragon’s dwelling with penetrating clarity.
When the dragon saw the reflections of the three Buddhas as before, he thought, "The reflections of three Buddhas have appeared in the world; there can be no further Buddhas."

The dragon was greatly delighted; emerging from the water, he looked around to his left and right and saw the Buddha sitting beneath a tree, his body endowed with the thirty-two marks, of a pure golden hue, as upright and majestic as the sun and moon.
The Buddha’s thirty-two marks appeared from afar like a tree in full bloom.
The Naga King Manasvin then approached the Buddha and circumambulated him seven times.
Having seven heads, he spread them over the Buddha’s head as a canopy.

The dragon emerged from the water to attend upon the Buddha, and for seven days there was wind and rain. For seven days the Buddha remained in dhyāna, neither moving nor shaking, neither breathing nor pausing; the Buddha’s mind was supremely blissful and boundless.
After seven days had passed, the wind and rain ceased.
Because the Buddha had attained the Way for the first time, he rejoiced and did not eat for seven days; seeing the Buddha’s joy, the dragon also attended upon him and did not eat for seven days.
When the seven days had ended, the Buddha awakened of his own accord; the nāga then transformed himself into a young brahmin, knelt with palms joined, and asked the Buddha, "Are you not cold?"
“Have you attained freedom from fever?
Have you attained freedom from being harassed by insects, moths, mosquitoes, and gadflies?
The Buddha replied:
The Sūtra says:
"A person finds joy in a secluded place.
What I previously heard, I have now seen all through direct experience; this is what brings joy.
It is blissful to dwell in the world without being harassed by others;
it is also blissful not to harass people of the world or the classes of wriggling and flying creatures;
and it is further blissful to transcend them, no longer becoming a person of the world nor a deva.
"It is also blissful to be free from anger, hatred, and lust;
it is also blissful to attain the path of the Buddha’s Nirvana within this world.
The dragon addressed the Buddha, saying:
"From this day forward, I take refuge in the Buddha and take refuge in the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the dragon, "In the future, there shall be many arhats and the community of bhikṣus; you should likewise devote yourself to taking refuge in them as well."

Among the animals, Man-lin was the first to take refuge in the Buddha. The Buddha’s supernormal powers were thoroughly penetrating; when the devas assembled, they all bowed their heads and came forward to pay their respects.
The Buddha, dwelling in seclusion in a quiet place, reflected with focused mindfulness:
"I feel deep compassion for all beings throughout the world and desire to instruct them; whom should I teach first?
My King sent five men to attend upon me, yet these five were unable to keep pace with me. They are now by the water's edge; I shall teach them first."
The Buddha then returned by way of his original path.
When the five men saw the Buddha coming from afar, they did not know who he was and said to one another:
"If this man comes, be careful not to pay him homage; be careful not to speak with him."
The five men all said, "We may!
and the Buddha heard from afar what the five men had spoken.
When the Buddha arrived, the five men were all struck with awe and fear; they stepped forward and paid homage to the Buddha.
The Buddha said, "You five men, for what reason do you lack firm resolve?"
His own attendants said to him,
"Be careful not to pay obeisance to this man who is coming.
Why, then, do you now pay obeisance?
The five men did not dare speak again.
The Buddha took the five men with him and traveled for several days; then, the Buddha stroked their heads and beards with his hand, and they all became śramaṇas.
There were three practitioners of the Way, each instructing disciples: one practitioner taught five hundred disciples;
another practitioner taught three hundred disciples;
and another practitioner taught two hundred disciples, totaling one thousand people.
The Buddha, leading five śramaṇas, arrived at the place where the three practitioners resided; all the disciples were filled with great joy and followed the Buddha.
As the Buddha led his disciples traveling through various kingdoms and reached the city gates, the bells and drums sounded of their own accord, and the lutes and harps chimed spontaneously.
The sick were healed, the aged became youthful again, the blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the hunchbacked were straightened, and the lame were able to walk.
The hundred beasts harmonized their mournful cries;
the devas flew down and scattered flowers, performing music above him.
The Buddha’s light illuminated countless heavens, and his domain encompassed three thousand suns and moons, with twelve thousand worlds and earths all belonging to him.
Throughout his life, he instructed disciples before and after [his teaching], teaching tens of millions of billions of people, all of whom attained the Way and were delivered from the world.
From the *Pusa benqi jing* (Sutra on the Original Arising of the Bodhisattva).
